Chapter 6: Refining Mindfulness—Working with Subtle Obstacles and Deepening Practice.
As you get more familiar with mindfulness, you might start to notice that some obstacles aren’t as obvious as they used to be. Maybe it isn’t restlessness or clear distraction anymore. Instead, these new challenges sneak in quietly, and if we’re not careful, they can chip away at the depth and stability of your practice.
But here’s the thing: running into these subtler obstacles actually means you’re making progress—not falling behind.
One sneaky roadblock is expectation. Once you’ve been practicing for a while, it’s only natural to hope for certain results—maybe a sense of calm, a flash of insight, or even something spiritual. But when we start holding on to these hopes, we create tension and set ourselves up for disappointment.
Mindfulness, at its core, is about meeting each moment just as it is—not how we wish it would be. So, when you notice expectations popping up, see if you can gently recognize them and let them go. Then, come back to the simple awareness of what’s happening right now.
Another subtle challenge that often comes up is the desire for progress. Maybe your mind starts comparing today’s meditation with yesterday’s. Or you find yourself measuring up to some imagined standard of how meditation “should” feel. This habit of comparing can lead to frustration, or even a bit of self-criticism.
Instead, try showing up with what’s called a beginner’s mind—open, curious, and not weighed down by the need to achieve something every time you sit.
Doubt is another visitor that can show up in more refined ways. Even after months, or years, of practice, it’s normal to wonder, “Is this actually working? Am I doing it right?” Rather than pushing these doubts away, see if you can include them in your awareness. Notice them with the same gentle curiosity you’d give to any thought or feeling.
So, how do you work with these subtler obstacles? Here are a few down-to-earth strategies:
First—try noticing any subtle resistance. If boredom, impatience, or a hint of aversion pops up, just acknowledge it. You might quietly say to yourself, “Ah, boredom is here,” and then return to your breath.
Second—let go of striving. Remind yourself, there’s nowhere you have to get to, and nothing you have to achieve. The real value is in the practice itself, not in reaching some perfect state.
And third—when things feel tangled or complicated, just come back to basics. Notice your breath, feel your body, and let the simplicity of the moment anchor you.
As you keep practicing these skills, your mindfulness becomes steadier and less tied to what’s happening around you. The mind learns how to rest in awareness itself—no matter what’s going on. It’s a bit like learning to sit quietly by a river, watching the water flow by, without feeling the need to change its course.
Over time, your practice deepens. You’ll notice more moments of clarity and calm, and those old patterns of thought and reaction might start to loosen their grip. It’s not a straight path—there’ll be ups and downs, easy stretches and tough ones. But the key is to approach each phase with patience and kindness, trusting that understanding will unfold, little by little, as you continue.
